job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in structural engineering at Ashford University and I live at home in Greystone village, forty minutes away, with my parents. My dad is a builder with a crew of six, and I've been on his sites since I was fourteen. Most days I go to lectures or the computer lab, and in the evenings I help dad price jobs. I did my bachelor's in civil engineering, top of the class, with a summer at a bridge design firm and a placement as a site engineer on a school extension. My fiancée Hannah is a primary teacher, and we go to church together on Sundays. I do my calculations by hand first and I don't use AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I never believed all that talk. Buildings are built by people with boots and brains, and no program has ever poured a slab. I'd tell the men at dad's yard that the world still needs builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty content. Civil engineering is steady work, there's a lot of repair and building to do, and I know the local firms. My concern is the usual one: I want to marry Hannah next summer and I'd like a salary before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to the bridge firm where I interned and two construction companies, and ask my old site manager, Mr Dlamini, to put in a word. I'd keep pricing jobs for dad on weekends. We'd set the wedding date and save about 300 a month between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know where I'm going and who I'm going with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about the wedding if work didn't come through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to wait a year, and Hannah's parents would be polite about it. Dad would offer me work on his crew, and I'd take it, though I'd hate to waste the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about working for your dad in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud and a bit trapped. I love the sites, but I want to do the structural side, which his firm can't give me. I'd do it for Hannah and not complain.

say: Buildings are built by people with **boots and brains**, and no program has poured a slab.
think: Civil engineering is **steady work**, and I know the local firms.
My concern is a **salary** before the wedding next summer.
do: Apply to the bridge firm where I interned and two **construction companies**.
Keep pricing jobs for **dad** on weekends.
feel: **Calm**, because I know where I'm going and who with.
S0.quote: Buildings are built by people with boots and brains, and no program has ever poured a slab.
fieldNote: Liam's calm comes from a **trade** he has known since fourteen, local contacts and a clear plan for his wedding.
His one worry is **timing**: a salary before marrying Hannah next summer.

steps.text: Apply to the bridge firm and two construction companies
Keep pricing jobs for dad's crew on weekends
Set the wedding date and save 300 a month with Hannah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office side that changes and not the site side. Drawings, calculations and checking get done by software, but a building needs a person to look at the ground and decide. I'd keep my head down and not argue online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy. The jobs for graduates are mainly in the design office, and that's exactly the work that software takes first. I think the firm that hired me might take two juniors where it used to take five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my effort into site-based roles, such as site engineer, where you need to be there. I'd try an AI tool once, reluctantly, on a past calculation, to see what mistakes it makes. And I'd ask Hannah's uncle, who runs a surveying firm, whether he'd take me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not angry, I just want it to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you try a tool you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To know what I'm up against. My dad says you can't fight a machine you've never seen run. I'd do it in secret first, on a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the church or community could offer in that kind of world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People help each other in my church: someone finds you a job, someone brings food. It isn't a plan, but it's a net, and I'd lean on it before the government.

say: The **office side** changes, not the site side, because a building needs a person to look at the ground.
I'd keep my head down and not argue online.
think: Graduate jobs are mainly in the **design office**, which software takes first.
The firm might take **two juniors** where it used to take five.

Try an **AI tool** once on a past calculation.
feel: **Uneasy**, not angry, wanting it to settle.
S1.quote: My dad says you can't fight a machine you've never seen run.
fieldNote: Liam's reluctance toward AI softens into **practical scouting**: he tries a tool secretly to learn its weaknesses.
He trusts **church and family** as a safety net before government help.

steps.text: Apply for site engineer roles with local builders
Test one AI tool on my old bridge calculation one Sunday
Ask Hannah's uncle if his surveying firm takes graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years isn't enough, and I don't trust anyone who says they have a plan. I'd tell people to look after their families and communities first. And I'd say the government should stay out of the way but protect the basics, like food and housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. The design work I trained for would go, and Hannah and I would be starting out in the middle of it. My dad's crew is probably safe until the robots catch up around 2031, but he's sixty and his knees are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever structural or site job turns up straight away, and move into dad's crew if nothing does. I'd move the wedding forward, because I'd want to be married before things get hard. I'd save every spare cent, about 400 a month, and ask the church about practical help for young couples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady in my faith. I'd keep my head and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bring the wedding forward. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the world's going to be strange, I want to face it with Hannah. We'd have a small ceremony and skip the big party. It would save about 3,000 as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll learn the crew's work properly. He'd pretend he didn't need me, but he would.

say: Two years isn't enough, and I don't trust **anyone** who says they have a plan.
Look after your **families** and communities first.
think: The **design work** I trained for would go, just as Hannah and I start out.
My dad's crew is safe for now, but his **knees** are going.
do: Take any structural or **site job** straight away.
Move the **wedding forward** to a small ceremony.
Save **400 a month** and ask the church about help.
S2.quote: If the world's going to be strange, I want to face it with Hannah.
fieldNote: Liam answers a crisis with **family and faith**: an earlier wedding, his father's crew and the church's practical help.
He distrusts **planners** more than the technology, a traditional reflex.

steps.text: Take any structural or site engineer job offered within a month
Bring the wedding forward to a small ceremony this spring
Save 400 a month and skip the big party
Ask the church about practical help for young couples

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get on with it. I'd tell people to learn a trade and have a family, and not put life on hold. I'd say employers should keep taking apprentices and young engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but hopeful. By 2031 I'd be 29, married, maybe with a child, with a job and a bit of land to my name. If robots come to building sites in 2034, I'd already be a site manager, not a labourer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a graduate job, work towards a site manager's licence, and finally use an AI tool for the paperwork. I'd save 350 a month and put a deposit on a small house. I'd also work with dad on an extension business, so we have something of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. I can see a decent life inside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use an AI tool. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. In five years it's normal, and a site manager who does paperwork by hand looks silly. I'd rather learn it now, on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the house mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A place near dad and Hannah's parents, a garden, and a mortgage I can manage. It's my idea of safe.

say: Five years is long enough to **get on with it**, so learn a trade and don't put life on hold.
think: By 2031 I'd be **29**, married, maybe with a child and a job.
As a site manager I'd be ahead of the **robots** in 2034.
do: Take a graduate job and work towards a **site manager's** licence.
Save **350 a month** for a house deposit.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, because I can see a decent life inside it.
S3.quote: A site manager who does paperwork by hand looks silly.
fieldNote: Liam's resistance to AI **cracks** once the date is real, and he calls it learning on his terms.
A **house near family** is his picture of safety.

steps.text: Take a graduate site engineer job and start the site manager licence
Learn an AI tool for site paperwork and scheduling
Save 350 a month for a house deposit near our parents
Start an extension business with dad on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because there's time to do things properly. I'd tell friends to marry, buy a house and not be bullied by headlines. I'd say we've heard promises about machines before and I'd want to see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. By 2036 I'd be 34, with two or three children and a trade in my hands. The world might change, but there's a decade to get settled and tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at the design firm and on dad's crew, and save for a house. I'd get a chartered licence by 30. I'd also teach apprentices on Saturdays, because I think the trade needs people who care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite content. It's an ordinary life, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want your life to look like at thirty-four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house in Greystone village, three kids, and Sunday lunch with both families. And a decent job that doesn't take my evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd keep to yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd still like to be proven wrong about AI. I'd love to say it was all hype, and I'm a little afraid it isn't.

say: There's time to do things **properly**, so marry, buy a house and ignore headlines.
think: By 2036 I'd be **34** with a family and a trade in my hands.
A decade is enough to get **settled** and tested.
do: Finish the master's and work at the design firm and on **dad's crew**.
feel: **Calm** and content, because it's an ordinary life.
S4.quote: I'd still like to be proven wrong about AI. I'd love to say it was all hype, and I'm a little afraid it isn't.
fieldNote: Liam is **calm** because a decade fits his picture of an ordinary life with family and trade.
His private confession is a **hope** to be wrong about AI, mixed with fear he isn't.

steps.text: Marry Hannah and plan for three children
Save for a house in Greystone village
Earn a chartered engineer licence by age thirty
Teach apprentices on Saturdays at dad's yard

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time for my marriage and career to settle before it hits. What would help is apprenticeships for young engineers, support for families starting out, and employers who still hire people who can work on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not the type to say I'm afraid. I'd rather be asked straight, and I'd answer straight.

headlineQuote: I'm not the type to say I'm afraid. I'd rather be asked straight, and I'd answer straight.
portrait: Liam is a 24-year-old **civil engineering** graduate doing a master's, living at home and engaged to a primary teacher.
He grew up on his father's building sites, goes to church and prefers **family and community** to government help.
He avoids AI tools, but a real date makes him say he would **learn them** on his terms.
His mood stays calm in mild cases and turns **anxious** at two years, when his wedding and design work are at stake.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time for his marriage and career to settle.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for young engineers, support for new families and employers who hire for site work.
